{{Short description|American evolutionary ecologist}}
'''Duncan Irschick''' (born 1969 in San Francisco, California) is an evolutionary ecologist and functional morphologist in the field of animal athletics, more specifically known as animal performance. He has worked on many kinds of animal species, including [[reptile]]s and [[amphibian]]s, [[rodent]]s, [[ungulate]]s, [[spider]]s, and [[human]]s. He was a faculty member at [[Tulane University]] for five years (2001–2006) before joining the faculty at the [[University of Massachusetts at Amherst]] in 2006.

==Early life==
He earned his B.S. in [[Zoology]] from the [[University of California, Davis]] in 1991. He earned his Ph.D. from [[Washington University in St. Louis]] in 1996. He then went on to postdoctoral research at the [[University of Cincinnati]] and at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. During this period, he expanded his research to functional themes, including studies of [[Kinesiology|kinetics]], and [[kinematics]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bio.umass.edu/biology/about/directories/faculty/duncan-j-irschick|title=Duncan J. Irschick|date=28 September 2009 |publisher=University of Massachusetts at Amherst|accessdate=March 14, 2019}}</ref>

==Career==

===Research===
Duncan Irschick is most well known for his work on [[gecko]] adhesion, and rapid evolution.<ref>{{cite news|author=Judson, Olivia|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2008/07/22/a-natural-selection/|title=A Natural Selection Science Writer|date=July 22, 2008}}</ref> He along with several colleagues, conducted the first test of how much force a gecko toepad could produce. Their recorded value of 20 Newtons of force for two front limbs<ref>Irschick, D. J., Austin, C. C., Petren, K., Fisher, R. N., Losos, J. B., Ellers, O. 1996. A comparative analysis of clinging ability among pad-bearing lizards. Biological Journal of the Linnean Society 59:21-35.</ref> for a [[Tokay gecko]] was a starting point for a large body of research on bioadhesion and synthetic production of gecko [[setae]], which has captured significant attention in the public eye.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://science.discovery.com/videos/weird-connections-the-sticky-gecko.html |title=Discovery Channel Cable Show about Gecko Adhesion, which includes some of Duncan Irschick's work |access-date=2009-06-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090603083238/http://science.discovery.com/videos/weird-connections-the-sticky-gecko.html |archive-date=2009-06-03 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2012, he, together with colleagues from the University of Massachusetts published a paper<ref>{{cite journal|author=Michael D. Bartlett|author2=Andrew B. Croll|author3=Daniel R. King|author4=Beth M. Paret|author5=Duncan J. Irschick|author6=Alfred J. Crosby|title=Biomimetics: Looking Beyond Fibrillar Features to Scale Gecko-Like Adhesion (Adv. Mater. 8/2012)|journal=Advanced Materials|year=2012|volume=24|issue=8|page=1078|doi=10.1002/adma.201290037|bibcode=2012AdM....24..994B |doi-access=}}</ref> describing the invention of "Geckskin", which shows some elements of the anatomy of geckos, and for which a 100&nbsp;cm<sup>2</sup> piece can hold up to 700&nbsp;lb on a smooth surface, yet can be peeled off with little effort, which was widely covered in the popular media.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://phys.org/news/2012-02-gecko-feet-scientists-super-adhesive-material.html|title=Inspired by gecko feet, scientists invent super-adhesive material|website=[[Phys.org]]|date=February 16, 2012|accessdate=March 14, 2019}}</ref>

In 2004, he, along with several other colleagues, completed a study showing that rapid evolution (36 years) of a major body part (a cecal valve of the intestinal tract in Croatian squamates can occur, apparently due to invasion of a novel island habitat.<ref>Herrel, A., Huyghe, K., Vanhooydonck, B., Backeljau, T., Breugelmans, K., Grbac, I., Van Damme, R., Irschick, D. J. 2008. Rapid large scale evolutionary divergence in morphology and performance associated with the exploitation of a novel dietary resource in the lizard ''Podarcis'' ''sicula''. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 105:4792-4795.</ref> This study, published in the [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]] in 2008, has been presented as evidence for [[evolution]] in modern times.<ref>Richard Dawkins. The Greatest Show on Earth: The Evidence for Evolution. Free Press (United States), Transworld (United Kingdom and Commonwealth). 2009. {{ISBN|0-593-06173-X}}.</ref><ref>Zimmer, Carl The Tangled Bank: An Introduction to Evolution(2009) {{ISBN|0-9815194-7-4}}.</ref>

===Editorial===
Duncan Irschick is a senior editor for the journal ''[[Functional Ecology (journal)|Functional Ecology]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.functionalecology.org/view/0/editorialboard.html|title=Editorial Board|publisher=Functional Ecology|doi=10.1111/(ISSN)1365-2435 |accessdate=March 14, 2019}}</ref> and an associate editor for ''[[The Quarterly Review of Biology]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/journals/qrb/board?mobileUi=0&|title=The Quarterly Review of Biology|publisher=University of Chicago Press|accessdate=March 14, 2019}}</ref> He has served on several other editorial boards as a faculty member.

==Recognitions==
He has been named as the Hilgendorf lecturer for the [[University of Tübingen]] in 2010,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://uni-tuebingen.de/en/faculties/faculty-of-science/departments/biology/institutes/evolutionecology/eve-phds/everest/everest-events/hilgendorf-lecture/|title=The Hilgendorf Lecture|accessdate=March 14, 2019|archive-date=August 5, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805134400/https://uni-tuebingen.de/en/faculties/faculty-of-science/departments/biology/institutes/evolutionecology/eve-phds/everest/everest-events/hilgendorf-lecture/|url-status=dead}}</ref> and as the OCIB lecturer for the [[University of Ottawa]] in 2008. He has been awarded several grants from the [[National Science Foundation]] and the [[National Institutes of Health]].
